      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Ovarian Cysts</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The ovaries are part of the female reproductive system. They produce a woman's eggs and make female hormones. <span class="qt0">Ovarian cysts</span> are fluid-filled sacs in or on an ovary. They usually form during ovulation, when the ovary releases an egg. They are usually harmless and go away by themselves. Most women have them sometime during their lives.</p><p>Most <span class="qt0">ovarian cysts</span> are small and don't cause symptoms. Women may not find out that they have them until they have a pelvic exam. If there are symptoms, they may include:</p><ul><li>Pressure</li><li>Bloating</li><li>Swelling</li><li>Pain in the lower abdomen, on the side where the cyst is</li></ul><p>If your health care provider finds a cyst, you may be able to wait to see if it gets bigger. You may need surgery if you have pain, are past menopause, or if the cyst does not go away. If a cyst bursts or causes bleeding, you should get medical help right away. Birth control pills can help prevent new cysts.</p><p>Rarely, <span class="qt0">ovarian cysts</span> can become cancerous. This risk increases as you get older.</p><p>A health problem that involves <span class="qt0">ovarian cysts</span> is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).  Women with PCOS can have high levels of male hormones, irregular or no periods, and small <span class="qt0">ovarian cysts</span>.</p><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ovariandisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Ovarian Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ovarian Insufficiency</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are ovaries?<p>The ovaries are a pair of female reproductive glands that make eggs and female hormones. Women have one ovary on each side of the uterus (where a fetus grows during pregnancy). Each ovary is about the size and shape of an almond.</p><p>Ovaries play a role in menstruation, pregnancy, and menopause.  Your ovaries:</p><ul><li>Produce and store eggs that are released during ovulation (when an egg leaves the ovary and travels into the fallopian tube). If a sperm fertilizes the egg, you can become pregnant.</li><li>Make the female hormones estrogen and progesterone.</li><li>Stop making those hormones and releasing eggs during menopause.</li></ul><p>Some medical problems can affect the ovaries. These can cause various symptoms, and some ovarian disorders may need prompt treatment.</p>What are the types of ovarian disorders?<p>Some problems that can happen with the ovaries can include:</p><ul><li>Ovarian cancer is when a cancerous tumor forms in the tissues of an ovary.</li><li><span class="qt0">Ovarian cysts</span> are fluid-filled sacs in or on an ovary.</li><li>Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a set of symptoms related to an imbalance of hormones.</li><li>Primary ovarian insufficiency is when your ovaries stop working before age 40.</li><li>Ovarian torsion is a twisting of the ovary.</li><li>Endometriosis is when tissue like the lining in your uterus grows in other places in your body. It may affect the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and tissue lining the pelvis.</li><li>Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infection and inflammation of the uterus, ovaries, and other female reproductive organs.</li><li>Ovarian tumors.</li></ul>What causes ovarian disorders?<p>Ovarian disorders can happen for different reasons depending on the condition. Sometimes the cause is unknown.</p>What are the symptoms of ovarian disorders?<p>Your symptoms may be different, depending on the problem with your ovaries. Some ovarian disorders, such as <span class="qt0">ovarian cysts</span>, may cause few or even no symptoms. Other disorders may cause more severe symptoms. Symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Pelvic pain, which often happens during your period</li><li>Nausea or diarrhea</li><li>Vaginal bleeding that is between periods, very heavy, or longer than usual</li><li>Vaginal discharge</li><li>Painful menstrual cramps</li></ul>How are ovarian disorders diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have a problem with your ovaries, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Will ask about your family health history</li><li>Will do a physical exam, including a pelvic exam</li><li>May order imaging tests, or blood tests</li></ul>What are the treatments for ovarian disorders?<p>Treatment depends on the ovarian disorder, your symptoms, overall health, and plans for pregnancy. Treatment can include medicines, such as pain relievers or hormonal birth control, lifestyle changes to reduce symptoms, or sometimes surgery. Ovarian cancer may require surgery, chemotherapy, or other targeted therapy.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/polycysticovarysyndrome.html">
      <content name="title">Polycystic Ovary Syndrome</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">PCOS</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Stein-Leventhal Syndrome</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)? <p>Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), also known as polyendocrine metabolic ovary syndrome (PMOS), is the name of a hormonal disorder. PCOS affects the ovaries, as well as many other parts of the body.</p><p>If you have PCOS, you usually have at least two of these problems:</p><ul><li>Not ovulating. Normally, your ovaries make the egg that is released each month as part of a healthy menstrual cycle. This is called ovulation. But with PCOS, the egg may not develop as it should, or it may not be released during ovulation. Your periods may be irregular, or you may not have them at all.</li><li>High levels of androgens. Androgens are hormones that are important for normal male sexual development. Women normally make smaller amounts of androgens. Having higher levels of androgens can cause you to have extra body or facial hair (called hirsutism).</li><li>Growths in one or both ovaries. These growths are often clumps of ovarian follicles that have stopped developing. They may appear as cysts, which are small fluid-filled sacs</li></ul><p>Although it's less common, you may not have growths in your ovaries. You may only have symptoms of PCOS, not ovulate, and have high levels of androgens.</p>What causes polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>The exact cause of PCOS is unknown. Research has shown that different factors may play a role, including:</p><ul><li>Genetics. PCOS tends to run in families.</li><li>Imbalances in androgen levels.</li><li>Insulin resistance. This is a condition in which your body can't use insulin properly. Insulin is a hormone that helps move blood glucose (also called blood sugar) into your cells to give them energy. Insulin resistance can lead to high blood glucose levels.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>PCOS often develops as young as age 11 or 12, around the time of your first period. But you can develop it later.</p><p>The symptoms can vary from person to person. Some women have few or even no symptoms. They may not realize they have PCOS until they have trouble getting pregnant. Other women may have more severe symptoms.</p><p>The symptoms of PCOS may include:</p><ul><li>Irregular or missed menstrual periods.</li><li>Too much hair on the face, chest, stomach, or thighs.</li><li>Obesity, weight gain, or trouble losing weight.</li><li>Severe acne which may be hard to treat.</li><li>Oily skin.</li><li>Patches of thickened dark skin (called acanthosis nigricans).</li><li>Infertility. PCOS is one of the most common causes of infertility. But many women with PCOS can still get pregnant.</li></ul>What other health problems are linked to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>PCOS is linked to many other health problems, including:</p><ul><li>Insulin resistance, which can lead to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.</li><li>Heart disease. Having PCOS increases your risk, and this risk goes up as you age.</li><li>High blood pressure.</li><li>High LDL ("bad") cholesterol and low HDL ("good") cholesterol. This increases your risk of heart disease.</li><li>Endometrial hyperplasia, a condition in which the lining of your uterus, or womb, becomes too thick. This can increase your risk for endometrial cancer, also called uterine cancer.</li><li>Sleep apnea, a disorder that causes you to repeatedly stop breathing during sleep.</li><li>Depression and anxiety.</li></ul><p>Although there are links between PCOS and these conditions, researchers do not know whether:</p><ul><li>PCOS causes some of these problems</li><li>Some of these problems cause PCOS, OR</li><li>There are other conditions that cause both PCOS and these other health problems</li></ul><p>Not everyone who has PCOS will have all these problems. However, you and your health care provider may want to monitor your health for signs of them, so they can be treated early.</p>How is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for PCOS. To find out if you have PCOS, your provider: </p><ul><li>Will do a physical exam, which will include looking for the physical signs of PCOS.</li><li>Will ask about your medical history and family health history.</li><li>May do a pelvic exam to check for signs of extra male hormones and to see if your ovaries are enlarged or swollen.</li><li>May order a pelvic ultrasound to look for growths on your ovaries and check the thickness of your endometrium (the lining of your uterus, or womb).</li><li>May order blood tests, including tests to check your hormone levels.</li></ul>What are the treatments for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>Treatments for PCOS can help you manage your symptoms. The treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Lifestyle changes, which can help reduce many symptoms. They can also lower your risk for or help manage related health problems. These changes include:
  <ul><li>Maintaining a healthy weight</li><li>Getting regular physical activity</li><li>Eating healthy foods</li></ul>
</li><li>Medicines:<ul><li>Hormonal birth control, such as pills, shots, and IUDs, can make your period more regular. They may also help remove acne and extra facial and body hair. But it's only an option if you're not currently trying to get pregnant.</li><li>Anti-androgen medicines, which block the effect of androgens. This can help reduce hair loss on your head, the growth of facial and body hair, and acne. Providers do use them to help with these symptoms, but anti-androgen medicines are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat PCOS. These medicines can cause problems during pregnancy. Your provider may have you take them with birth control (to prevent pregnancy).</li><li>Insulin-sensitizing medicines, which are medicines that are used to treat type 2 diabetes. They improve insulin resistance and keep your blood glucose levels steady. They may also lower your androgen levels. They are not approved by the FDA to treat PCOS. But they may help with your symptoms.</li><li>Medicines for acne. These medicines come in pills, creams, or gels.</li></ul></li><li>Treatments for hair removal, such as facial hair removal creams, laser hair removal, and electrolysis.</li><li>Fertility treatments if you are having trouble getting pregnant. They include medicines and procedures such as in vitro fertilization (IVF).</li></ul></content>
